title: Trump Imposes Up to 100% Tariffs on Drone Imports to Counter China
excerpt: The new tiered tariff structure targets Chinese-made drones with militarily sensitive capabilities while offering lower rates to allies, as the administration moves to reshore drone manufacturing ahead of a September meeting with Xi Jinping.
body:
• Larger drones with military-sensitive features like thermal imaging face a 100% tariff from China, while smaller drones face 25%. US allies face rates between 10% and 15%.
  • The tariffs, imposed under Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act, are considered more legally durable than other Trump tariffs invalidated by the Supreme Court earlier this year.
  • China dominates over half of the US commercial drone market through manufacturers like DJI, making this a direct challenge to Beijing's tech sector ahead of the expected Trump-Xi meeting on September 24.

President Donald Trump on Thursday announced sweeping tariffs on imported drones and their components, imposing duties of up to 100% on Chinese-made unmanned aerial vehicles in a move aimed at breaking Beijing's grip on the commercial drone market and reshoring production to the United States.

The White House said the drone tariff program would protect US national and economic security while creating jobs. "U.S. drone production needs to be expanded rapidly to ensure U.S. national and economic security," the administration said in a statement.

How the Tariffs Work

The tariffs are tiered by drone capability and country of origin. Larger drones with militarily sensitive features — such as thermal imaging — face a 100% tariff based on their value, along with certain critical components. Smaller drones and components without direct national security implications face a 25% levy.

US allies will pay significantly lower rates. Drones from the European Union, Japan, South Korea, Switzerland, Taiwan, and Liechtenstein face a 15% tariff. The United Kingdom faces a 10% duty, contingent on substantially all hardware, software, and technology originating from the UK or US.

These allied rates align with trade deals secured last year that capped many US tariffs at 15% — and 10% for the UK — in exchange for concessions on tariffs and regulations on American goods. The drone tariffs on allied nations will not stack on top of other existing levies.

Legal Basis and Timing

The action was taken under Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962, which allows the president to impose tariffs to address national security risks. This is the same provision Trump has used for tariffs on steel, aluminum, and automobiles in his second term — levies that survived a Supreme Court decision in February that invalidated many of his other global tariffs.

The Commerce Department last year conducted an investigation into foreign-made drones and found that reliance on imports threatened national security. The proclamation also authorizes the commerce secretary to establish an onshoring program for companies investing in domestic drone manufacturing.

The tariffs take effect 21 days after the proclamation's signing, with duties on less sensitive components kicking in after 180 days.

Why Drones, Why Now

Chinese manufacturers, led by DJI, account for more than half of all US commercial drone sales. The conflict in Ukraine has demonstrated drones' central role in modern warfare, making domestic production capacity a strategic imperative.

"U.S. drone production needs to be expanded rapidly to ensure U.S. national and economic security."

— White House statement

The move comes ahead of an expected September 24 meeting between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping, adding another pressure point to the already tense trade relationship. It also follows recent Federal Communications Commission restrictions on some foreign-made drones and separate bans on power inverters and robots from China.

Congressional support for action against Chinese drones has been bipartisan. The American Drone Manufacturing Dominance Act of 2026, introduced by Rep. Pat Harrigan (R-NC), would set aside $1.5 billion in federal funding to accelerate removal of Chinese-made drones from law enforcement and subsidize a domestic manufacturing base.

Impact on Indian Drone Industry

For India's growing drone sector, the tariff structure creates a potential opening. Indian drone manufacturers could benefit from the gap left by restricted Chinese imports, particularly as New Delhi has been investing heavily in its own drone ecosystem under the Production Linked Incentive scheme. However, Indian-made drones would face the general tariff rates absent a specific bilateral trade agreement with the US.

Trump separately signed a National Security Presidential Memorandum aimed at fixing long-term issues in Navy shipbuilding and restoring capacity to the maritime industrial base.
nri_angle: India's growing drone industry could benefit from the gap created by restricted Chinese imports, as Indian manufacturers look for openings in the US market.
